text:
I have been thinking this week about the difference between knowing where the risk is and actually doing something about it.

My team published one piece on the StoneComms business page this week, and it sits right in that gap.

Africa is getting much better at mapping climate risk. Heat, flooding and other hazards can now be described at useful levels of detail. But a good map is still only information. The real test is whether it changes a budget, a design, an operating rule or somebody's responsibility.

That matters financially because adaptation money is scarce. Africa needs at least US$70 billion a year for adaptation, while tracked flows reached US$14.8 billion in 2023. When the gap is that large, every pound or dollar needs to be able to answer a fairly basic question: what risk is this reducing, for whom, and how will we know?

It matters ethically for the same reason. Climate risk is not experienced as a map. It is experienced as a school that is too hot, a market that floods, a clinic that fails, or a neighbourhood that keeps paying for the same damage. Better data is useful only if institutions are able — and required — to act on it.

Our researchers propose treating climate data as decision infrastructure: linking place, thresholds, exposed people and services, the actual decision, the institution responsible, the finance and the result.

That sounds procedural. It is. But procedure is often where good climate evidence either becomes action or quietly disappears.
